source.title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning in Large Language Models with One Training Example
source.authors: Yiping Wang; Qing Yang; Zhiyuan Zeng; Li-Liang Ren; Li-Yuan Liu; Baolin Peng; Hao Cheng; Xuehai He; Kuan Wang; Jian-Feng Gao; Weizhu Chen; Shuo-Hang Wang; S. Du; Ye-Long Shen

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream generalization after RLVR training on one or a few examples in large language models, a new setting relative to the mapped versions.
record.gate_note: Reports test performance after RLVR training on natural math examples, including comparisons with format-reward and larger-dataset training. The study does not test random-label memorization alongside natural-label generalization, nor the interventions or measurements named in V2–V8.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out reasoning performance after one- or few-example RLVR, but tests none of V1–V8. Its corrupted-label experiments do not establish near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels or chance-level held-out performance. Post-saturation training trajectories do not test widening beyond interpolation. The connection to double descent and implicit regularization is speculative.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that selected one- or few-example RLVR can substantially improve reasoning and sometimes match training on thousands of examples. They interpret this as activating capabilities already present in pretrained models, identify policy-gradient loss as the main contributor, and emphasize exploration and data selection. They also report post-saturation generalization; their proposed implicit-regularization mechanism remains a hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GRPO or PPO reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards on language models and math prompts; not the standard gradient-method settings or interventions in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Training example choice; base model; RL algorithm; entropy-loss coefficient; rollout temperature; label correctness; prompt complexity; evaluation checkpoint and evaluation length.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected one- or two-example RLVR runs substantially improve Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B benchmark accuracy and approach larger-dataset RLVR; gains vary across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RLVR on selected natural math examples can improve pretrained language models' held-out reasoning performance, sometimes approaching training on thousands of examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Training accuracy saturates before step 100, while six-benchmark accuracy subsequently improves by 3.4 points for π1 and 9.9 points for π13 over the stated intervals; strong test performance persists after training outputs become incoherent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In one-example RLVR, held-out performance can improve after training accuracy saturates and remain strong despite later deterioration in training-response coherence.

fits_no_version.finding: Policy-gradient loss produces most of the gains; exploration settings, label correctness, and prompt complexity affect outcomes. Substantial gains persist with partially corrupted labels without demonstrating random-label fitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few-example RLVR performance depends on training signals and example choice, and is partly robust to corrupted reward labels.

record.problems: The study focuses mainly on mathematical reasoning and models up to 7B, with limited coverage of other domains and larger models. It reports no uncertainty intervals for the extracted benchmark values. Results depend on example choice, checkpoints and model; the authors note training instability for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. It does not measure the generalization constructs in V1–V8.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: per-benchmark results for every model, example, checkpoint and evaluation length in Tables 3, 4, 9–13 and 17–20; response-length, pass@8, judge-agreement, and reflection-word measurements. These are outside the claim versions' stated measures or would exceed the 60-row cap. Figure-only training/test trajectories in Figures 1–2 and 5 were not reconstructed into numeric rows.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level held-out accuracy for random labels under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning conditions and recovery interventions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, including training-set size, excessive dropout, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing measures.
Removing examples selected by label-memorization influence versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, not denials of the reported benchmark gains. No version-specific verdict is warranted. The omitted training trajectories are declared in rows_left_out and concern a finding outside these versions, so they do not require a missing entry. Reported outcomes generally use checkpoints selected for benchmark performance.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with held-out performance on natural labels for the same architecture and recipe.
Does not sweep network width past the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD under the version's tuning conditions.
Does not compare batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with other generalization measures.
Does not identify and remove memorized training examples.
